title: The effects of cannabis on nicotine use: Integrating human laboratory and ecological momentary assessment methods
text:
Co-use of nicotine and cannabis poses a substantial public health risk, including a higher prevalence of health-
related, psychiatric, and psychosocial problems and poorer cessation outcomes for both substances, relative to
single-substance use; however, the impact of cannabis on nicotine use behavior is poorly understood. The
proposed project will use a novel, multimodal approach that integrates a systematic and rigorous laboratory
model with ecological momentary assessment to examine cannabis’s effects on electronic nicotine delivery
systems use in young and emerging adults who use both substances. Findings from this project will provide a
more comprehensive understanding of how cannabis and nicotine interact and inform targeted, substance-
specific prevention and treatment approaches.

title: The University of Kansas Cancer Center
text:
OVERALL: PROJECT NARRATIVE 
The University of Kansas Cancer Center (KUCC) aims to leverage unique regional scientific assets to build a nationally significant cancer research center that will become a leading institution for transforming discoveries in the laboratory into new therapeutic approaches. KUCC will expand its depth, breadth and impact and strive to become an NCI-designated comprehensive cancer center that meets the needs of the more than 4.5M Americans who live within the 92,000 square miles of the KUCC catchment area.

title: Using DNA hydrogels to mimic, exploit, and fundamentally investigate extracellular matrices
text:
The influence of tissue mechanics on cell behavior has been widely acknowledged, especially in the contexts of
wound healing, disease advancement, and regenerative medicine, however, there is a critical shortage of
materials that can effectively elucidate the intricate relationship between tissue mechanics and cellular
responses. In this proposal, our primary goal is to enhance the applicability of hydrogel biomaterials by
harnessing clinically approved plasmid deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) to create materials that emulate the
properties of living tissues. This approach will allow us to integrate unique structural and functional attributes
inspired by the versatile and dynamic characteristics of DNA enabling fundamental understanding of cell-
environment homeostasis research and facilitating transition into clinical applications.

title: Interactions of retroviral and host proteins guided by advanced modeling
text:
Viruses are efficient machines that seize normal cellular functions for their own benefits. The
application of new computational approaches has sparked life into challenging projects and now
allows difficult questions relating to viral receptor usage and integration to be addressed.
Identification and characterization of these host proteins and the development of targeted
inhibitors to them has broad implications for public health, both as it relates to viral pathogenesis
as well as diseases relating to gene and oncogene expression.

title: Standardizing and Harmonizing Behavioral and Social Science Research Factors in Alzheimer's Disease through Ontology-Based Approaches
text:
Our proposed strategy utilizes both ontology and NLP methods to streamline ADRD-related BSSR data
standardization and integration. By establishing a shared ontological framework and employing NLP for
information extraction, we aim to foster interdisciplinary collaboration among researchers from diverse fields,
facilitating a more comprehensive understanding of ADRD and its behavioral and social aspects. This
integrated approach improves data quality, accessibility, and the ability to uncover insights critical to ADRD
research.

title: Targeting NADH-Reductive Stress in Mitochondrial Disease
text:
Inherited mutations in mitochondrial genes cause multiple devastating neuromuscular diseases
that have no FDA-approved therapies. Here, we are investigating whether correcting a common
biochemical consequence of mitochondrial diseases, known as “NADH-reductive stress”, using
our novel enzyme tool named LOXCAT, has therapeutic benefits. Our proposal will pave the way
for novel therapies for various incurable mitochondrial diseases.

title: 5D subcellular imaging for cell biology
text:
We propose to develop subcellular imaging tools with minimal photobleaching and photodamage by
novel optics, photophysics and advanced analysis, which will facilitate to reveal structures and dynamics
of proteins and RNAs within living cells in three-dimensional space, time and multicolor (5D).

title: 3D Scanning Two-photon Fiberscope Technology for Simultaneous Multi-region Multi-cell-type Imaging in Freely-moving Rodents
text:
This proposal aims to develop a new 3D-scanning two-photon fiberscopy imaging technology, which will
overcome the challenges in currently available brain imaging technologies and allow for assessment of
functional and dynamic connectivity of neural networks from different brain regions with high-resolution in
freely-moving animal models (e.g., rodents). Successful development of the proposed technology could
potentially accelerate the process of uncovering general principles of neural circuits in a working brain.

title: Mechanisms and Therapy of Radiation Resistance in Breast Cancer
text:
This proposal seeks to understand mechanisms that contribute to resistance to radiation therapy in aggressive
breast cancers and to use the information obtained to improve therapy. The specific focus is neuropilin-2
(NRP2), a specific receptor for vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) that has a major role in promoting
radiation resistance, and for which specific, inhibitory mAbs are available for clinical use.

title: Immunologic and Predictive Features of MIS-C
text:
Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) is a disease caused by SARS-CoV-2
virus. Clinically it manifests 4-6 weeks after initial SARS-CoV-2 infection. The
pathophysiological determinants are largely unknown, as is the ability to assess the relative risk
of disease development, disease diagnosis and prognosis.

title: Understand & overcome resistance to PD-1
text:
Narrative, Project 2: Characterizing and overcoming failure to respond to PD-1 blockade therapy
Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) is an aggressive skin cancer driven either by the Merkel cell polyomavirus or by UV-
mutations, and about half of patients with advanced MCC persistently respond to PD-1 blockade. During the current
Project 2 funding period, we identified a strong biomarker of response (the number of circulating cancer-specific T cells)
and several therapeutically addressable immune evasion mechanisms that are now advancing to clinical trials linked to
this P01. Project 2 will engage expert collaborators to analyze powerful sets of biospecimens derived from clinical trials
to achieve its goals: 1) Identify clinically feasible biomarkers of PD-1 response in MCC and 2) identify and overcome
innate and adaptive mechanisms that mediate resistance to PD-1 pathway blockade.

title: Molecular factors governing the biogenesis and release of short immunostimulatory RNAs
text:
Defense against microbial infections relies on a variety of cellular and molecular mechanisms, including those
involving short non-coding RNAs (sncRNAs). We recently found that specific tRNA-derived sncRNAs accumulate
abundantly in macrophages during immune activation and act as potent endogenous immunostimulatory ligands,
yet the mechanisms that generate and export these molecules remain poorly defined. In this project, we will
dissect how a subset of RNA helicases, together with a cargo-selecting RNA-binding protein, orchestrate the
release and intercellular delivery of immunostimulatory tRNA-derived sncRNAs, thereby defining an sncRNA-
mediated pathway that contributes to innate immune regulation.

title: Enhancements to the GMOD Suite of Genome Annotation and Visualization Tools
text:
The mission of GMOD and JBrowse is to make genome data accessible using the tools
of the dynamic web. The size of genomic datasets can be daunting to users, particularly
as the number of sequenced species and strains proliferates. We propose to add
machine learning tools to help navigate these datasets, along with user interface
enhancements that exploit evolutionary similarity, and improvements to performance
and usability via a series of benchmarks and outreach operations.

title: Learning How to Give Casual Explanations for Large Scale Virtual and Morphological Pharmacology
text:
Recent advances in biotechnology and computing are unlocking complex model systems including single-cell
morphological profiling and large-scale virtual screening for pharmacology discovery. To get the most out of
these complex model systems, my group develops machine learning and statistical methods to infer the causal
mechanisms. Two projects that embody this work include modeling how spatial factors explain and confound
cellular morphology and mapping bioactive chemical space to guide adaptive virtual screening.

title: Cancer Epidemiology
text: PROJECT SUMMARY – Cancer Epidemiology (CE) Program The mission of the Cancer Epidemiology (CE) Program is to investigate the determinants of cancer risk and progression through epidemiological studies strongly grounded in the relevant biology. The program also includes the development of novel biostatistical approaches that incorporate complex biological measures from population-based studies to elucidate mechanisms and pathways. The CE program is led by Christopher Haiman ScD, a cancer and genetic epidemiologist whose research is focused on genetic risk of prostate and breast cancer, and V. Wendy Setiawan PhD, an expert on cancer risk factors, disparities, and big data linkages whose research focuses on liver, pancreas and endometrial cancer. The program has 25 members who collaborate within CE and throughout NCCC to accomplish three Specific Aims: 1) Elucidate the role of genetic factors in cancer etiology and outcomes with emphasis on different populations; 2) Elucidate the role of environmental and lifestyle factors in cancer etiology; and 3) Develop and apply methods for integrative statistical analysis of ‘omics’ data in environmental and genetic epidemiology research in cancer. During this funding cycle, CE members made major novel discoveries including: 1) identification of potentially carcinogenic molecular signatures in e-cigarette users; 2) elevated risk of pancreatic cancer among individuals with late-onset diabetes in African Americans and Latinos; 3) cytomegalovirus as a novel risk factor for acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and multiple myeloma (MM); 4) demonstration that exposure to air pollution is a risk factor for breast and brain cancer and is associated with decreased survival; 5) development of a multiethnic polygenic risk score for prostate cancer that is being translated to a clinical study with collaborators in the TACS Program; and 6) identification of disparities in prevalence of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and its role as risk factor for liver cancer among community populations. Through effective evaluation and planning, CE established new Program goals, catalyzed intra- and inter-programmatic collaborations, and fostered effective junior faculty mentorship. During the current grant period, CE investigators published 607 papers, of which 33% are intra- programmatic, 20% are inter-programmatic, 76% are multi-institutional, and 26% are high impact (IF >9). Members hold $13.5M in cancer-relevant funding, of which $12.2M is peer reviewed and $6.4M is NCI funding (directs). The CE Program contributes critically to NCCC’s mission of decreasing the cancer burden in the catchment area through knowledge of etiologic risk factors underlying cancer disparities.

title: Reversing Immune Dysfunction for HIV-1 Eradication
text:
While antiretroviral therapy (ART) has achieved remarkable success, with AIDS patients now living long, full
lives, HIV-1 infection remains incurable due to the presence of a persistent viral reservoir, capable of rebounding
upon interruption of treatment. The RID-HIV (Reversing Immune Dysfunction for HIV-1 eradication) Collaboratory
brings together leading university scientists from more than twelve academic institutions as well as Merck
Research Laboratories, with the goal to understand the molecular and cellular basis for the loss of immune
homeostasis in HIV infected patients. This knowledge will be harnessed to create a therapeutic paradigm
encompassing immune restorative treatments, utilized in concert with enhanced viral reactivation and elimination
strategies, to establish a HIV-1 cure.

title: Immunology Research Program
text: IMMUNOLOGY PROGRAM The Immunology Program (IMM) is devoted to enhancing our understanding of the function of the innate and adaptive immune system in the pathogenesis of malignant disease. There are four specific aims: (1) Elucidate new roles for innate immune receptors and the microbiome in carcinogenesis; (2) Uncover novel functions of diverse immune cells and pathways in the tumor microenvironment; (3) Develop novel approaches to use immunotherapy to treat patients with cancer; (4) Discover new targets for improving the outcome of patients with malignant disease undergoing allogeneic stem cell transplantation (allo-SCT). There are 24 program members from six different departments at UNC School of Medicine. Members have $13.2M (direct costs) cancer-related funding including; $2.8M in direct costs from NCI and $6.8M in in direct other peer and other NIH. NCI funding has increased 145% since the last submission. Highlights of the program include discoveries of new roles of innate immune receptors in colorectal cancer; importance of microbiota on cancer-relevant immune cell populations; a comprehensive immunogenomic characterization of the tumor microenvironment for TCGA and critical roles for T follicular helper and B cells during checkpoint inhibitor therapy in breast cancer. Significant translational findings include the new use of antigens expressed on solid tumors as targets for chimeric antigen receptor modified T cell therapy (CAR T) including B7-H3 for pancreatic cancer and glioblastoma, and CD138 for multiple myeloma. IMM is led by Jenny Ting PhD, William Rand Kenan Professor of Genetics, Microbiology-Immunology (M-I) and Director of the Translational Immunology Center who is a world’s expert on innate immune receptors, and Jonathan Serody MD, Elizabeth Thomas Professor of Medicine, M-I and the Associate Director for Translational Sciences in the Cancer Center, who is an expert on the biology of GVHD, tumor vaccines and the tumor microenvironment. IMM leadership works closely with CR to translate findings from IMM. These include the evaluation of CD30-specific CART T cells in the treatment of CD30-expressing lymphomas, B7-H3-specific CAR T cells in relapsed ovarian cancer and GD2-specific CAR T cells in neuroblastoma. Six outstanding faculty members have been recruited since the last grant submission. IMM has a strong publication record with 359 papers; 18% intra-programmatic, 39% inter-programmatic publications and 33% of the papers were in journals with an impact factor > 10. IMM has a strong record of training with two training grants focused on tumor immunology or immunotherapy. Research within IMM has been significantly informed by the Office of Outreach and Community Engagement with an emphasis on cancers in the catchment area, including breast, colorectal, pancreatic cancers and multiple myeloma.

title: Limited Competition: National Biocontainment Laboratories (NBLs) Operations Support (UC7 Clinical Trials Not Allowed)
text:
The Galveston National Laboratory (GNL) Operational Support Program ensures the continued
availability, safety, and modernization of high-containment research facilities essential for the
discovery and development of next-generation medical countermeasures, diagnostics, and
vaccines against biological threats of national security concern. This project directly supports
national priorities by promoting biosafety, biosecurity, artificial intelligence integration, and
responsible biotechnology innovation. Sustaining this critical infrastructure enables rapid
response to emerging infectious disease outbreaks and bioterrorism events, thereby protecting
the health and security of the nation and the global community.

title: Derivation of lung epithelia from iPS cells for advanced disease modeling
text:
Lung diseases, such as pulmonary fibrosis, result in significant morbidity and mortality worldwide.
The advent of stem cell discoveries and regenerative medicine presents new opportunities to
improve our understanding of these diseases and to develop new treatment approaches. Here
we propose to better understand the pathogenesis of and develop new therapies for interstitial
lung diseases and pulmonary fibrosis, based on new in vitro models of disease that utilize patient-
specific pluripotent stem cells.

title: Commercializing nanodroplet technology to improve diagnostic sensitivity for difficult-to-lyse microbial samples
text:
The above aims will help Triangle advance SnapLyse to commercialization by enabling scalable manufacturing,
providing independent validation by R2D2 TB and feedback in the context of existing clinical algorithms, and
completing the studies necessary for regulatory submission. At the conclusion of this CRP, Triangle will submit
a diagnostic workflow for Mtb for FDA approval, thus preparing Triangle for commercial launch of the first
SnapLyse products. The development of this technology that enables effective extraction of DNA of resilient
microbes will facilitate earlier detection of disease, improve disease management and treatment, and prevent
disease outbreaks while increasing scientific rigor.
